_comment: Written in our own words from the NHS week-by-week guide to pregnancy (nhs.uk). Not reviewed by a health professional.

0.baby: Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last period, so the first two weeks come before conception. Around week 2 an egg can be fertilised, and by week 3 a tiny cluster of cells settles into the lining of the womb.
0.body: Most people don't notice anything yet, and a test won't show a result until around the time a period is missed.

4.baby: The embryo is about 2 mm long. A small sac of fluid surrounds it, and a yolk sac feeds it until the placenta takes over.
4.body: A missed period is often the first sign. Tiredness, tender breasts, nausea or needing to pee more are common, and some people notice light spotting.

5.baby: The brain, spinal cord and nervous system are taking shape, and the face is beginning to form. The tiny heart is forming and may start to beat around now.
5.body: Tiredness, sore breasts and needing to pee more often are common this week.

6.baby: Small buds appear that will become arms and legs, and the liver, brain and muscles are developing. Little dips mark where the ears will be.
6.body: Nausea can come at any time of day, and many people find their sense of smell gets stronger.

7.baby: The brain is growing faster than anything else, which gives the embryo a large forehead. Eyelids, nostrils and ear dimples are starting to form, and the arm buds are getting longer.
7.body: The volume of blood in your body is rising, which can leave you thirsty. Bloating and tiredness are common.

8.baby: The placenta is growing roots into the wall of the womb, and the head is beginning to straighten. From now on the embryo is called a foetus.
8.body: Bloating, slightly fuller breasts and mood swings are common. The growing womb can press on your bladder.

9.baby: The face is easier to recognise, with eyelids, a mouth and a tongue. Hands and feet are forming, and the main organs and bones are developing.
9.body: Pregnancy hormones are near their peak, which can make you feel unwell or more emotional than usual.

10.baby: The baby makes small jerky movements that can be seen on a scan, far too small to feel. The ears, upper lip and the buds of the first teeth are forming.
10.body: Bloating, heartburn and indigestion are common, and many people feel very tired.

11.baby: Fingers and toes are separating, and tiny nails are starting to grow. The body is growing quickly.
11.body: Stretching muscles and ligaments can cause aches around the bump, and extra blood flow can make you feel hot or dizzy.

12.baby: The skeleton is turning from soft tissue into bone, and the organs and muscles are in place. The heartbeat can be picked up on an ultrasound.
12.body: Nausea often starts to ease and appetite returns, as the placenta takes over from the early hormones.

13.baby: The baby is about 7.4 cm long, and its movements are becoming more deliberate. It may suck its thumb, which builds the sucking reflex it will need to feed.
13.body: A small bump may start to show. The need to pee often eases as the womb rises out of the pelvis.

14.baby: The head is rounder and better in proportion with the body. The baby is now passing small amounts of urine into the fluid around it.
14.body: Many people feel their energy start to come back around now.

15.baby: Fine soft hair covers the body, and eyebrows and eyelashes are forming. Hearing is beginning: the baby may pick up your voice, your heartbeat and the sounds of your digestion.
15.body: Itchy skin and a little more clear or white discharge are common.

16.baby: The face makes its first expressions, though not yet on purpose. The arms and legs move, and the hands can make fists.

17.baby: The eyes can move behind closed lids, and the baby reacts to loud sounds. Fingernails are growing and fingerprints are forming.
17.body: Your waist starts to disappear as the womb rises. First movements are often felt between weeks 18 and 24, as bubbling or fluttering.

18.baby: Hearing, touch, swallowing and sucking are all developing, and there is plenty of wriggling. In many places a detailed scan is offered between weeks 18 and 21.
18.body: Your blood pressure may dip a little, so standing up slowly can help. A dark line down the middle of the belly is common.

19.baby: The baby is putting on weight, and the adult teeth are forming behind the first set.
19.body: Pregnancy hormones loosen your ligaments, so some movements may feel less comfortable than before.

20.baby: From about now the baby is measured from head to heel, and is about 25.6 cm long. A protective greasy coating covers the skin, and the baby is more active each day.
20.body: You may start to feel bubbling or fluttering movements. Leg cramps at night are common.

21.baby: The baby can hear sounds and voices from outside the womb, and is practising sucking and breathing movements. Regular patterns of sleeping and waking are settling in.
21.body: As your centre of gravity shifts you may feel less steady on your feet, and backache and tiredness are common.

22.baby: The lungs are developing, and the baby swallows small amounts of the fluid around it. Taste buds are forming.
22.body: Stretch marks may start to appear on the belly, thighs or breasts.

23.baby: The limbs are now in proportion with the body. Over the coming weeks kicks will get stronger and may be visible from the outside.
23.body: Your ribs may ache as your rib cage widens, and you may feel a little short of breath.

24.baby: The baby has normal proportions but is still much smaller and thinner than at birth.
24.body: Aches around the ribs, back and hips are common as your ligaments loosen.

25.baby: The baby is active, may startle at loud noises, and can get hiccups.
25.body: Slight puffiness in the face, hands or feet is common; mention it to your midwife, who may want to check your blood pressure.

26.baby: The eyes open for the first time, and the baby is learning to blink.
26.body: Leg cramps at night, tiredness and a little forgetfulness are common.

27.baby: The lungs are maturing, and the baby is filling out with fat.
27.body: Bloating, constipation and snoring are common at this stage.

28.baby: The baby is about 37.6 cm from head to heel, and the heart beats around 140 times a minute.
28.body: Heartburn, backache and swollen ankles are common. Swelling of your face, hands or feet is worth having checked by your midwife.

29.baby: The organs are maturing and the baby keeps building fat. The greasy coating on the skin starts to fade.
29.body: As the baby presses up towards your lungs you may feel breathless, and you may need to pee more at night.

30.baby: The eyes can now focus. After birth, the baby will see faces best at about 20 to 25 cm away.
30.body: Sleep can be broken, and vivid dreams are common.

31.baby: The baby is plumper and less wrinkled, very active, and can start to recognise voices from outside.
31.body: Practice contractions, painless tightenings that last 20 to 30 seconds, are common from around now.

32.baby: The baby still has around a kilogram of fat to gain in the coming weeks, and is probably head-down by now or will be by about week 36.
32.body: Walking may feel harder as the bump grows. Movements should keep their usual pattern right up to birth; if they slow down, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away.

33.baby: The brain and nervous system are fully developed. The bones of the skull stay soft and separate, which helps at birth.
33.body: A heavy feeling low in the pelvis can mean the baby has turned head-down. Only about 1 in 20 babies arrive on their due date.

34.baby: The baby lies curled up with the knees towards the chest, and may be moving down into the pelvis.
34.body: Your breasts may leak a little early yellow milk, called colostrum. Some earlier discomforts can ease as the baby drops.

35.baby: The baby is getting chubbier, which will help it keep warm after birth. Movements should stay as strong and regular as before.
35.body: Kicks can make your ribs sore.

36.baby: The lungs are probably mature enough to breathe without help, and the baby can suck and digest milk.
36.body: Leaking a little urine when laughing or coughing is common as the pelvic floor relaxes.

37.baby: The baby is practising facial expressions, and its active and calm times are easier to tell apart. About 95 in 100 babies are head-down by now.
37.body: More discharge, practice contractions and an urge to clean and tidy are common.

38.baby: Most of the fine body hair has gone, and the bowel is storing the baby's first poo, called meconium.
38.body: Waiting can feel long; this is normal. Your midwife keeps checking your blood pressure and urine.

39.baby: The skin is firmer, and the greasy coating may still be there at birth or may have gone.
39.body: Backache, pressure low in the bump and bursts of energy are common. A small plug of mucus, called a show, can come away as the body gets ready.

40.baby: The baby has little room left but should keep its usual pattern of movements.
40.body: Practice contractions are frequent, and period-like aches or low backache can be early signs of labour.

41.baby: Most babies weigh about 3 to 4 kg by now and have finished their fast growth. Skin can look dry and peeling once the greasy coating has gone.
41.body: Going up to a week past the due date is common. From 41 weeks your care team will usually talk with you about extra monitoring or helping labour to start.
